hints: Remember when real gases deviate most, think about high pressure, low temperature, and strong forces between particles.
Compare the four gases for polarity and hydrogen bonding, and notice that both $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ can hydrogen bond.
Ask which gas is closest to turning back into a liquid at $150^{\circ}\text{C}$, since being near its boiling point means intermolecular forces are still very important.
walkthrough:
**Recall when gases are ideal**

An ideal gas assumes no forces between particles and negligible particle volume. Real gases deviate most at low temperature, high pressure, and when they have strong intermolecular forces.

Ideal assumptions: no IMF, elastic collisions

**Compare polarity and forces**

Fluorine ($\text{F}_2$) and krypton ($\text{Kr}$) are non-polar with only weak London forces, so they behave quite ideally. Ammonia ($\text{NH}_3$) and steam ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$) are both polar and form hydrogen bonds, so both will deviate more.

**Check closeness to liquefaction**

Deviation is greatest close to the boiling point, where a gas is about to condense. At 101 kPa, water boils at $100^{\circ}\text{C}$, so steam at $150^{\circ}\text{C}$ is only $50^{\circ}\text{C}$ above condensing. Ammonia boils at $-33^{\circ}\text{C}$, far below $150^{\circ}\text{C}$, so it is much more ideal.

Therefore steam, with strong hydrogen bonding and a temperature closest to its liquefaction point, behaves least like an ideal gas.

options.A: Ammonia is polar and hydrogen bonds, so it does deviate, but its boiling point is $-33^{\circ}\text{C}$. At $150^{\circ}\text{C}$ it is well above liquefaction, so particles have high kinetic energy to overcome attractions. It is less non-ideal than steam.
options.B: Fluorine ($\text{F}_2$) is a small non-polar molecule with only weak London forces and a very low boiling point ($-188^{\circ}\text{C}$). At $150^{\circ}\text{C}$ it is far from condensing and behaves very much like an ideal gas.
options.C: Krypton is a noble gas, monatomic and non-polar with only weak London forces. It has no permanent dipole or hydrogen bonding and a very low boiling point, so at $150^{\circ}\text{C}$ and 101 kPa it behaves almost ideally.
options.D: Steam ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$) is polar with very strong hydrogen bonding. Its boiling point is $100^{\circ}\text{C}$, so at $150^{\circ}\text{C}$ it is only just above condensation. Intermolecular attractions are still significant, giving the greatest deviation from ideal behaviour.
